terms.short: Sell straight away at the best bid
terms.definition: To sell immediately at the highest price a buyer is showing, instead of waiting for a better price. It gets you out fast but gives up the spread.
examples: News is out and it's falling; just hit the bid on the lot.
terms.fill: You need to sell right now, so you ____ at 412 instead of offering at 413.
wrong: Raise your buying price to attract sellers
Place a buy order below the market
Cancel a bid you left earlier

calcs.q: The bid is 100.10 and the offer 100.20. You hit the bid for 5,000 shares. What do you receive?

terms.short: Buy straight away at the best offer
terms.definition: To buy immediately at the lowest price a seller is showing. It's the buyer's version of hitting the bid: fast, but you pay the spread.
examples: Someone's lifting every offer in Infosys; there's a big buyer around.
terms.fill: You must buy before the news, so you ____ at 250 rather than bidding 249.80.
wrong: Sell at the highest bid
Withdraw your offer to sell
Raise the price you're asking to sell at

calcs.q: A stock is quoted 249.80 / 250.00. You lift the offer for 2,000 shares. What does it cost?
calcs.why: Lifting the offer means buying at 250.00: 250 × 2,000 = ₹5,00,000.

terms.short: A quote with both a bid and an offer
terms.definition: A quote showing both the price you'd buy at and the price you'd sell at, so the other side can choose. Asking for a two-way hides whether you want to buy or sell.
examples: Show me a two-way in the Bank Nifty December future.
terms.fill: To avoid revealing whether you're a buyer or a seller, ask the broker for a ____.
wrong: A quote valid for two days
A trade that goes through two brokers
A price agreed by both exchanges

calcs.q: A broker shows you 412.50 / 413.00 in size. If you buy and then sell straight back, what do you lose per share?
calcs.why: You buy at the offer (413.00) and sell at the bid (412.50): the 50 paise spread.

terms.short: Quantity of an order or position
terms.definition: Desk shorthand for quantity. 'What size?' asks how many shares or lots, and 'in size' means a large amount, enough to move the price.
examples: There's a buyer in size in Tata Steel; he's been lifting offers all morning.
terms.fill: When a broker says a fund wants to buy 'in ____', it means a large quantity.
wrong: The market value of a whole company
The gap between the bid and the offer
The tick by which prices move

terms.short: Filling a big order bit by bit
terms.definition: Carrying out a large order gradually over hours or days, buying or selling in pieces so the price isn't pushed too far. Brokers say they're working an order for a client.
examples: We're working a large sell order in HUL; don't be surprised if it's heavy all day.
terms.fill: A broker selling a fund's 20 lakh shares slowly through the day is ____.
wrong: Placing one market order for the whole amount
Checking an order for mistakes before sending it
Cancelling and re-entering an order

terms.short: A trade that has been reported
terms.definition: A trade that has gone through and shows up in the market data, especially a large one. Traders watch big prints for clues about who is buying or selling.
examples: Big print in Reliance at 1,412, about 8 lakh shares.
terms.fill: A single trade of 10 lakh shares flashing across the screen is a big ____.
wrong: A research report in paper form
A broker's daily statement
A price the exchange publishes before the open

terms.short: Context on who's trading what, and why
terms.definition: Information from brokers and traders about what's happening behind the prices: who is buying or selling, how big, and the story driving it. 'What's the color on HDFC Bank?' asks for exactly that.
examples: What's the color on HDFC Bank? It's down 3% on no news.
terms.fill: You ask your broker for ____ when a stock moves sharply and you want to know who's behind it.
wrong: A chart setting that colours rising prices green
A credit rating shown in colour
Gamma's sensitivity to time

terms.short: Client buying and selling through a desk
terms.definition: The stream of buy and sell orders coming from clients through a broker's desk. 'Flow is better for sale' means clients have mostly been selling.
examples: Flows have been two-way in IT, but banks are seeing steady foreign selling.
terms.fill: The desk said client ____ was heavily on the buying side all morning.
wrong: The cash a company makes from operations
The speed of the exchange's systems
A chart line joining daily closes

terms.short: A broker's interest to buy or sell a stock
terms.definition: A desk's known interest in buying or selling a particular stock, often because it has a client order to fill. A broker 'axed to sell' has stock to offer and may give a good price.
examples: We're axed to sell L&T; if you're a buyer, we can work something out.
terms.fill: Your broker has a big client sell order in L&T, so it has an ____ to sell.
wrong: A cut in a stock's target price
A sudden fall in a stock
A rule that stops a trader from trading

terms.short: Holding no position
terms.definition: Having no position at all in something: neither long nor short. Traders go flat before big events when they don't want any risk.
examples: I'm flat Infosys into results; too hard to call.
terms.fill: You sold the last of your shares and have no short either, so you're ____.
wrong: Holding a position with no gain or loss yet
Trading a stock whose price hasn't moved
Holding equal amounts of two stocks

tf.s: Being flat means your trade so far today has made no profit or loss.
tf.why: Flat means you hold no position. You may already have booked a profit or a loss.

terms.short: All the positions a trader runs
terms.definition: All the positions a trader or desk is responsible for. 'Running a book' means managing those positions and their risk, and 'the book is long' means it gains if prices rise.
examples: My book is too long banks; I need to cut some before the RBI meeting.
terms.fill: A trader who looks after the desk's options positions is running the options ____.
wrong: A company's net worth per share
A file of client orders waiting to be sent
The exchange's record of daily prices

terms.short: Firms that invest money
terms.definition: The firms that invest money and buy research and trading services: fund houses, insurers, pension funds and hedge funds. Buy-side people decide what to own.
examples: She moved from broking to the buy side and now runs a midcap fund.
terms.fill: Fund houses and insurers that pay brokers for research and trading are the ____.
wrong: Brokers that execute orders for clients
Anyone placing a buy order
Investors who never sell

terms.short: Brokers and banks that sell services
terms.definition: The brokers and investment banks that sell services to investors: trading, research and deals. Sell-side analysts write the reports the buy side reads.
examples: Sell-side estimates for Infosys have come down 5% since the last results.
terms.fill: Brokers' research analysts and sales traders work on the ____.
wrong: Investors who are selling a stock
Fund houses that manage savings
The side of the order book with offers

terms.short: Person who decides what a fund buys
terms.definition: The person who decides what a fund buys, holds and sells, and answers for its returns. In global desks they're often called the PM, short for portfolio manager.
examples: The PM wants to add to HDFC Bank but not above 1,700.
terms.fill: The decision to buy 2% of the fund in Titan was made by the ____.
wrong: The person who places the fund's orders on the exchange
A broker who manages client accounts
The regulator's officer for mutual funds

terms.short: Person who studies companies and rates them
terms.definition: A specialist who follows a set of companies or a sector, builds forecasts and publishes reports with a view on whether to buy or sell. In India, research analysts must be registered with SEBI.
examples: The analyst cut his estimates after the weak margin guidance.
terms.fill: The ____ covering cement stocks expects margins to recover next year.
wrong: The person who places orders for a fund
An official who audits company accounts
A trader who spots chart patterns
terms.note: SEBI's Research Analysts Regulations require registration for anyone giving research or recommendations for a fee.

terms.short: Broker who takes funds' orders and shares color
terms.definition: The person at a broker who talks to fund dealers and managers all day, takes their orders, and passes on market color and flow. They link the client to the broker's trading desk.
examples: My sales trader says there's a large seller in Asian Paints.
terms.fill: Fund dealers call their ____ at the broker to place orders and hear what others are doing.
wrong: A shop employee who sells shares to the public
An analyst who writes company reports
An exchange official who settles trades

terms.short: Person who places orders for a fund or broker
terms.definition: In India, the person on a fund's or broker's desk who actually places and manages orders on the exchange, following the fund manager's or client's instructions.
examples: The PM decides; the dealer works the order through the day.
terms.fill: The fund manager wants 5 lakh shares; the ____ places the orders and watches the fills.
wrong: A company that sells cars and bikes
The person who decides what a fund should buy
A SEBI official who approves trades

terms.short: Arranges share sales, deals and mergers
terms.definition: A firm that helps companies raise money and do deals: share sales such as IPOs, large block sales, and mergers and acquisitions. SEBI's rules call them merchant bankers.
examples: Three investment banks are running the IPO.
terms.fill: A company planning an IPO hires an ____ to price it and find investors.
wrong: A bank that invests depositors' savings in shares
The RBI's arm for government bonds
A mutual fund that buys banks

terms.short: Trading with the firm's own money
terms.definition: Short for proprietary trading: a firm trading with its own money for its own profit, rather than executing for clients.
examples: The broker's prop desk was short the futures while clients were buying.
terms.fill: A broker's desk that takes its own risk with the firm's capital does ____.
wrong: Trading on behalf of retail clients
Buying property shares
Trading only in the pre-open session

terms.short: Fund that can short, use leverage and more
terms.definition: A pooled fund for wealthy and institutional investors that can go long and short, use leverage and derivatives, and charges a share of profits. In India most are set up as Category III AIFs.
examples: A long-short hedge fund was shorting the stock while buying its rival.
terms.fill: A fund for wealthy investors that can short stocks and use leverage is a ____.
wrong: A fund that only buys safe government bonds
A fund that guarantees it can't lose money
A bank's fund for hedging its loans
terms.note: Alternative Investment Funds have a minimum investment of ₹1 crore for most investors.

terms.short: Fund that can only buy
terms.definition: A fund that can only own securities and can't short them, so it makes money only when its holdings rise. Most mutual funds and insurers are long-only.
examples: Long-only money has been buying every dip in the banks.
terms.fill: A fund that can't short and only profits when its holdings rise is a ____.
wrong: A fund that holds stocks for at least a year
A fund that invests only in long bonds
A fund with no exit load

terms.short: Bank that holds securities for institutions
terms.definition: A bank that holds securities for large investors, settles their trades and handles dividends and corporate actions. Every foreign portfolio investor in India must have one.
examples: The FPI's custodian confirmed the shares arrived on settlement.
terms.fill: A foreign fund buying Indian shares keeps them with a ____, which also settles its trades.
wrong: The broker who places the fund's orders
A guard at the exchange building
The regulator for foreign investors

terms.short: The companies an analyst follows
terms.definition: The set of companies an analyst or broker follows and publishes on. Initiating coverage means publishing the first report on a company, with a rating.
examples: Kotak initiated coverage on the stock with a buy.
terms.fill: A broker that publishes its first report on a company is initiating ____.
wrong: Insurance that protects a portfolio
The share of shares held by the public
Media reports about a company

terms.short: Analyst's call: buy, hold or sell
terms.definition: An analyst's recommendation on a stock, such as buy, hold or sell. Indian brokers also use add and reduce for milder views.
examples: Rating cut to reduce from add; the valuation has run ahead.
terms.fill: Moving a stock from hold to buy changes its ____.
wrong: A credit agency's grade for a company's debt
The exchange's risk score for a stock
The stock's rank in the Nifty

terms.short: Where an analyst thinks the price will go
terms.definition: An analyst's estimate of where a stock should trade, usually in 12 months. The gap to today's price is the implied upside or downside.
examples: Target price raised to 1,850, about 20% upside.
terms.fill: The analyst's ____ of ₹960 implies 20% upside from ₹800.
wrong: The price where a trader takes profit
The highest price in the last year
The price set for an IPO

calcs.q: A stock trades at 800 and the target price is 960. What upside does it imply?

terms.short: Analyst raises the rating
terms.definition: When an analyst raises a stock's rating, for example from hold to buy. Raising the target price or earnings forecasts is also loosely called an upgrade.
examples: The stock jumped 4% on a double upgrade, from sell to buy.
terms.fill: The broker moved the stock from hold to buy: an ____.
wrong: A company moving to a bigger stock exchange
A rise in a company's credit card limit
A stock being added to the Nifty

terms.short: Analyst cuts the rating
terms.definition: When an analyst cuts a stock's rating, for example from buy to hold. Cutting the target price or forecasts is also loosely called a downgrade.
examples: Downgraded to sell after the margin miss; the stock is off 6%.
terms.fill: Cutting a stock from buy to hold is a ____.
wrong: A stock being moved to the T2T segment
A fall in a stock's price
A cut in a company's dividend

terms.short: Holding more than the benchmark does
terms.definition: Holding more of a stock or sector than its weight in the benchmark. Some brokers also use overweight as a rating meaning the stock should beat the market.
examples: We're overweight private banks and underweight IT.
terms.fill: The fund holds 11% in HDFC Bank against an index weight of 8%, so it's ____.
wrong: Holding a stock that has become too expensive
Owning more than 5% of a company
Using too much leverage

calcs.q: A stock is 8% of the benchmark and 11% of your fund. How overweight are you?

terms.short: Holding less than the benchmark does
terms.definition: Holding less of a stock or sector than its weight in the benchmark, or none at all. As a rating, it means the analyst expects the stock to lag the market.
examples: We've stayed underweight IT all year, and it's helped.
terms.fill: Holding no Reliance when it is 9% of the index makes you heavily ____.
wrong: Being short a stock
Holding a stock that has fallen a lot
Having too little margin

tf.s: A fund can be underweight a stock while still owning it.
tf.why: Underweight only means holding less than the benchmark weight.

terms.short: Management's call with analysts after results
terms.definition: A call where a company's management discusses its results and takes questions from analysts and investors. In India it's usually called the concall.
examples: On the concall, management said demand is picking up in rural India.
terms.fill: After the results, analysts quiz the CFO on the ____.
wrong: A broker's call to collect margin
The day results are announced
A call option on earnings

terms.short: Results better than expected
terms.definition: When a company's results come in above the consensus forecast. 'In line' means close to it; the stock's reaction also depends on guidance.
examples: A big beat on margins, but the stock is flat because guidance was soft.
terms.fill: Profit came in 15% above what analysts expected: a clear ____.
wrong: Results that match last year's
A company buying back its own shares
Profit higher than last quarter

calcs.q: Consensus EPS was 20 and the company reports 23. By how much did it beat?

terms.short: Results worse than expected
terms.definition: When a company's results come in below the consensus forecast. A miss often hits the stock, unless the market expected worse.
examples: Revenue was fine but it's a miss on margins.
terms.fill: Profit came in well below analysts' forecasts: an ____.
wrong: A late filing of results
Profit lower than last year
A drop in the stock on results day

tf.s: A stock always falls after an earnings miss.
tf.why: If the market expected worse, or guidance is strong, it can rise.

calcs.q: Consensus profit was ₹1,000 crore and the company reports ₹920 crore. By how much did it miss?

terms.short: Market paying a higher multiple
terms.definition: When investors start paying a higher valuation multiple for a stock or sector, for example its P/E rising from 20 to 30, usually because they see better growth or lower risk. The opposite is a de-rating.
examples: Defence stocks got a big re-rating once order books took off.
terms.fill: Earnings didn't change, but the P/E went from 20 to 30: a ____.
wrong: An analyst raising a rating
A credit agency raising a bond rating
A stock moving to a higher index

calcs.q: EPS stays at 50 and the P/E rises from 20 to 25. How much does the share price change?
calcs.why: Price = EPS × P/E: 50 × 20 = 1,000 becomes 50 × 25 = 1,250, a 25% rise.

terms.short: Plenty of eager buyers
terms.definition: When buyers are keen and keep raising their bids, so the price holds up or rises. 'Banks are well bid' means there's steady buying in bank stocks.
examples: PSU banks are well bid after the budget.
terms.fill: Every dip in pharma is being bought; the sector is ____.
wrong: Priced too high by analysts
Stuck at the upper circuit
Full of unfilled sell orders

terms.short: Sellers are in control
terms.definition: When sellers dominate and keep lowering their offers, so the price drifts down. 'IT is offered' means there's steady selling in IT stocks.
examples: Metals are offered all day; nobody wants to catch them.
terms.fill: Sellers keep lowering their prices in metals; the sector is ____.
wrong: Available in an IPO
On sale through an OFS
Quoted with a two-way price

terms.short: Keep paying up to get filled
terms.definition: To keep raising your buying price, or lowering your selling price, as the market runs away from you, just to get the trade done.
examples: Don't chase it; if we miss it at 410, we wait.
terms.fill: If you keep raising your bid as the stock runs from 400 to 420, you ____ it.
wrong: Buy a stock just after it falls
Follow another fund's trades
Sell a stock after a big rise

terms.short: Trade against a move
terms.definition: To trade against a move you think will reverse: selling into a rally or buying into a drop. 'Fade the gap' means betting an opening jump won't last.
examples: I'd fade this rally; it's all short covering.
terms.fill: You sell into a sharp rally you think will reverse: you ____ the move.
wrong: Slowly close a position
Let a position expire
Lose interest in a stock

terms.short: Exited because the stop-loss was hit
terms.definition: Taken out of a trade because the price reached your stop-loss. Traders say they got stopped out, often just before the price turned back.
examples: Got stopped out at 1,640, and of course it bounced to 1,700.
terms.fill: Your sell stop at 1,640 filled before the stock recovered: you were ____.
wrong: Banned from trading for a day
Halted by a circuit limit
Forced to stop trading by the broker

calcs.q: You short 400 shares at 600 with a stop at 615. You get stopped out at 615. Your loss?

terms.short: Cut part of a position
terms.definition: To sell part of a holding, not all of it, often to lock in some profit or reduce risk. The opposite is to add.
examples: We trimmed Titan after the run-up but still like it.
terms.fill: Selling a quarter of your Titan holding after a big rally is a ____.
wrong: Sell the whole position
Cut a stock's target price
Reduce brokerage costs

calcs.q: You hold 10,000 shares and trim a quarter. How many do you still hold?

terms.short: Close out a position or trade
terms.definition: To close out a position or a whole trade, often a large or multi-part one, usually step by step. 'Long unwinding' means longs being closed, pushing prices down.
examples: Funds are unwinding the pair trade after the merger news.
terms.fill: Closing out all four legs of an options trade over two days is an ____.
wrong: Open a new position
Take a break from trading
Roll a contract to next month

terms.short: Buying back shares that were sold short
terms.definition: Buying to close short positions. When many shorts cover at once, the buying can push the price up sharply, even without good news.
examples: The rally is mostly short covering; there's no fresh buying yet.
terms.fill: A stock jumps as traders who sold it short rush to buy it back: that's ____.
wrong: Selling more shares short
Insurance against a short position
Buying a put to protect a long

tf.s: Short covering can push a price up even with no new buyers who want to own the stock.
tf.why: Shorts must buy to close, and that buying lifts the price.

terms.short: Live stream of trades and prices
terms.definition: The live record of trades and prices as they happen. 'Reading the tape' means judging buying and selling pressure from that stream.
examples: The tape feels heavy; every bounce is getting sold.
terms.fill: Watching every trade as it prints to judge the mood is reading ____.
wrong: A recording of a company's earnings call
Red tape at the regulator
A chart of the last year's prices

terms.short: Broker takes the client's trade on its own book
terms.definition: A trade where the broker buys or sells with the client directly, using its own capital, at an agreed price. The broker takes on the risk of then unwinding the position.
examples: The fund wanted out at once, so the broker gave a risk bid on a principal basis.
terms.fill: The broker bought the whole block itself at 2% below market, a ____, and took on the risk.
wrong: A trade only the company's promoters may do
A trade made by the head of the desk
The first trade of the day

calcs.q: The last price is 500. A broker bids 2% below that for a client's 10 lakh shares on a principal basis. What does the client receive?

terms.short: Broker trades for the client, no risk taken
terms.definition: A trade where the broker acts only as the client's agent, buying or selling in the market for a commission and taking no price risk itself.
examples: We'll do it agency and work it over three days.
terms.fill: The broker works the order in the market for a commission and takes no risk: an ____.
wrong: A trade by a government agency
A trade done through a travel agent's account
A trade in shares of an AMC

terms.short: Your trade is confirmed
terms.definition: The words that confirm a trade has happened at the agreed price and size. Once a dealer says 'done', both sides are bound.
examples: 'Two lakh at 412?' 'You're done.'
terms.fill: The broker confirms your 2 lakh shares at 412 with: '____'.
wrong: You've used up your trading limit
Your account is closed
You should stop trading for the day

tf.s: 'Nothing done' means the order traded but the price isn't final.

terms.short: A price you can trade on right now
terms.definition: A price someone is committed to trade at if you accept it straight away. It's the opposite of an indicative price.
examples: That's a firm price for 5 lakh, good for the next minute.
terms.fill: If you can say 'done' and the trade is fixed, the broker gave you a ____.
wrong: A price fixed by the exchange for the day
The price of a company's first share sale
A price that can't go below a floor

terms.short: A rough price, not a commitment
terms.definition: A guide to where something might trade, given without a commitment. The final price can be different, so traders ask whether a quote is firm or indicative.
examples: It's only indicative, around 1,410; I'll come back with a firm level.
terms.fill: 'Around 1,410, depending on size' is an ____, not a price you can deal on.
wrong: The price an index shows
The price in the pre-open session
A price set by SEBI

terms.short: The market and its professionals
terms.definition: Shorthand for the financial market and the people who work in it, especially analysts. In India 'Dalal Street', the road where BSE stands in Mumbai, means the stock market.
examples: The street was expecting 12% growth; they did 9%.
terms.fill: When analysts' average forecast is quoted as the '____ estimate', it means the market's consensus.
wrong: A list of brokers approved by SEBI
The open-outcry floor of the NSE
Retail investors as a group

terms.short: Already reflected in the price
terms.definition: When news or an expected event is already reflected in the price, so the price barely moves when it actually happens.
examples: The rate cut was fully priced in; the market didn't budge.
terms.fill: Everyone expected the dividend, so it was ____ and the stock didn't move.
wrong: Recorded at the closing price
Approved by the exchange
Sold at a fixed price

tf.s: If good news is fully priced in, the stock usually jumps when it's announced.
tf.why: If it's priced in, the price has already moved, so it barely reacts on the day.

aliases: buy the rumour, sell the news
terms.short: Price falls on good news it already rose on
terms.definition: When a stock that rose ahead of an expected event falls once the event happens, as traders who bought the rumour take profits. In full: buy the rumour, sell the news.
examples: Classic sell the news: up 20% into the listing, down 8% on the day.
terms.fill: The stock rallied for weeks before the results, then fell on a good report: buy the rumour, ____.
wrong: Sell after reading a news report
A rule against trading on news
Sell before results are announced

terms.short: A stock in a steep, fast fall
terms.definition: A stock dropping sharply and quickly. 'Don't catch a falling knife' warns against buying it before the fall has clearly stopped.
examples: It's down 30% in a week; I'm not catching that falling knife.
terms.fill: Buying a stock that's down 25% in three days, before it settles, is catching a ____.
wrong: A stock that cuts its dividend
A short position that's losing money
A slow and steady fall

terms.short: Holding a long that's going against you
terms.definition: Being long a stock while it falls: you bet on a rise and the market went the other way. Traders use it to admit a losing position.
examples: I'm long and wrong on the metals; cutting it before it gets worse.
terms.fill: You bought before results and the stock fell 10%: you're ____.
wrong: Holding a stock for too many years
Using the wrong order type
Buying a stock for the wrong reasons but making money
